title: No Rank
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 28 of 40
content:
Danse spent the first week after banishment trying to turn Listening Post Bravo into a military post.

There were only two of us.

This did not discourage him.

He made an inventory.

Then a watch schedule.

Then a maintenance schedule for equipment we did not have.

On the third day I found a duty roster taped beside the bunker door.

0600: perimeter check.

0700: equipment maintenance.

0800: breakfast.

I stared at it.

“Danse.”

He was cleaning a rifle at the table.

“What?”

“We are two people in an underground box.”

“Yes.”

“Who is this roster for?”

“Us.”

“I decline.”

“You can’t decline breakfast.”

“Watch me.”

His jaw tightened.

I took the paper down.

Danse stood.

“Put that back.”

“No.”

“It provides structure.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you removing it?”

“Because you’re using structure like a tourniquet around your entire personality.”

“That is ridiculous.”

“Is it?”

He reached for the paper.

I held it behind my back.

Danse stared at me in disbelief.

“Give me the roster.”

“No.”

“This is childish.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because you apparently need practice surviving harmless disorder.”

His face became thunderous.

For one second I thought I had pushed too far.

Then he sat down.

Not because he agreed.

Because the fight went out of him.

“I don’t know what I’m supposed to do,” he said.

The quietness scared me more than anger.

I put the roster on the table.

Danse stared at it.

“For years, every day had a purpose. Even bad orders were something to push against. Now I wake up and…”

He gestured around the bunker.

“Nothing.”

“You’re alive.”

“That is not a purpose.”

“No.”

I sat opposite him.

“It can be enough for a while.”

He looked unconvinced.

So I changed tactics.

“What do you want for breakfast?”

Danse frowned.

“What?”

“Breakfast. Not what supplies dictate. Not what gives optimal calories. What do you want?”

“That is irrelevant.”

“Humor me.”

He looked at the shelves.

“Eggs.”

“We don’t have eggs.”

“Then why ask?”

“Because now we have an objective.”

His eyes narrowed.

“You’re mocking me.”

“Only a little.”

We left the bunker to trade for eggs.

It was absurd.

That was why it worked.

The nearest settlement had six chickens and one woman willing to part with eggs in exchange for weapon repairs.

Danse fixed three rifles, a shotgun, and a bent hinge while I cooked.

People stared at him without the Brotherhood insignia.

Some recognized him anyway.

Nobody shot.

That counted as progress.

We ate eggs beside a fire.

Danse took one bite and closed his eyes.

“Good?”

“Yes.”

“Worth abandoning the roster?”

“No.”

I laughed.

He looked at me over the tin plate.

Then, slowly, smiled.

That afternoon a settler asked him to help reinforce a wall.

Danse almost answered with rank.

I saw the word form.

He stopped.

“Danse,” he said instead. “Just Danse.”

The settler nodded and handed him a hammer.

I looked away so he would not see what the moment did to me.

We stayed until evening.

Danse taught two people how to brace the gate against a charging creature. He repaired a water pump. He showed a teenager how to clear a jammed rifle safely.

Nobody saluted.

Nobody called him Paladin.

He was useful anyway.

On the walk back, he was quiet.

“Tired?”

“A little.”

“Regret leaving the bunker?”

“No.”

I waited.

He added, “I liked helping.”

“I know.”

“It felt…”

“Like purpose?”

Danse gave me a warning look.

I smiled.

“Sorry.”

“No, you’re not.”

“No.”

At Bravo, the duty roster still sat on the table.

Danse picked it up.

For a moment I thought he would tape it back to the wall.

Instead he folded it and put it in a drawer.

Not destroyed.

Not obeyed.

Kept.

A choice.

That night, when I climbed into the narrow bunker bed, Danse stood beside it uncertainly.

“You can sleep here,” I said.

“We’re not on the Prydwen.”

“I noticed.”

“There’s no storm.”

“I also noticed.”

His mouth twitched.

He lay down beside me.

This time there was no excuse.

His arm came around my waist.

I rested against him.

“Danse?”

“Yes?”

“What do you want tomorrow?”

He thought for a long time.

Then said, “Coffee that doesn’t taste terrible.”

I laughed into his chest.

“Ambitious.”

“I’m starting small.”

The egg expedition became a pattern.

Not eggs specifically.

Choices.

For the first time in his adult life, Danse had to decide things nobody could grade.

What shirt to wear when there was no uniform requirement.

Whether to repair the western wall now or tomorrow.

Whether to spend an afternoon helping a settlement when no superior officer would record the result.

The first few weeks, he treated every choice like a test with an answer key I had hidden from him.

“Blue or gray?” he asked one morning, holding two shirts.

“Whichever you want.”

“That is not useful.”

“It is literally the question.”

“The gray is more practical.”

“Then gray.”

“But I prefer the blue.”

“Then blue.”

He glared.

I drank my coffee.

“Danse, I am not issuing wardrobe orders.”

“You could express a preference.”

“Fine. Blue makes your eyes look nice.”

He froze.

I took another sip.

“See? Terrible idea.”

He wore blue.

At the settlement, nobody cared what color his shirt was. They cared that the east gate had sagged after a storm and that Danse could look at the supports for fifteen seconds and tell them why.

“The lower brace is carrying too much load,” he said.

The settlement carpenter crossed her arms.

“That’s what I told him.”

She pointed at her husband.

He looked wounded.

Danse knelt and examined the joint.

“You were correct.”

The carpenter beamed.

Her husband sighed.

I leaned against the fence.

“Careful. Competence is his love language.”

Danse’s head came up.

The carpenter laughed.

Her husband nodded solemnly. “I can see that.”

Danse looked at me with murder in his eyes.

Later, while we were cutting new braces, he said, “You cannot tell strangers that.”

“Why?”

“Because it is private.”

“Your appreciation of competence?”

“You know what I mean.”

I did.

The fact that we were together.

Not secret exactly. But precious enough that Danse still handled it like equipment he feared dropping.

“You embarrassed?” I asked.

“No.”

“Worried?”

He considered.

“Yes.”

“About what?”

“That if people know you matter to me, they can use you.”

The answer was pure soldier.

I set down the saw.

“People could already tell.”

His face fell.

“What?”

“Danse. You look at me like I’m an unsecured fusion core whenever I walk too close to danger.”

“I do not.”

“You absolutely do.”

“That is not a recognizable expression.”

“It is to everyone except you.”

He rubbed a hand over his face.

I stepped closer.

“We can be careful without pretending.”

“I’m not good at pretending.”

“I know. That is why this is adorable.”

“Stop calling me adorable.”

“No.”

The carpenter called us back before he could continue.

We spent the afternoon rebuilding the gate.

Danse taught instead of taking over. He let the carpenter make decisions. He asked the teenager helping us what *they* thought about the brace angle and waited for the answer.

Watching him without rank was strange because so much of the command remained.

But command was becoming something else.

Not authority granted by an organization.

Competence freely offered.

Choice became a kind of physical therapy.

The first time I asked what he wanted for dinner, Danse answered, “Whatever is nutritionally adequate.”

I refused to cook until he picked something.

He accused me of being unreasonable.

I ate an apple in front of him.

Twenty minutes later he said, “Eggs.”

The victory was absurdly satisfying.

The next day he chose where to sit outside. The day after that he decided not to repair a loose shelf until morning even though the tools were already out.

Each decision was tiny.

Each one irritated him because there was no superior officer to confirm it was correct.

One evening he caught me watching him move a chair closer to the bunker lamp.

“What?”

“You picked the better reading spot.”

“I moved a chair.”

“Without authorization.”

Danse stared.

Then, very deliberately, he moved it another six inches.

“Reckless,” I said.

“Apparently.”

The next morning the duty roster remained in the drawer.

By the end of the second week, the schedule on the wall had been replaced by a scrap of paper that said only:

COFFEE

CHECK WESTERN SEAL

MAYBE WALK TO MARKET

Danse claimed this was also a schedule.

I claimed the word *maybe* disqualified it.

He left it up anyway.

That felt like progress.

On the way home, we found a merchant with a crate of old paperbacks. Danse stopped.

I noticed.

“You want one?”

“No.”

“You stopped.”

“I was reading the titles.”

“Which is the first stage of wanting one.”

He sighed.

Ten minutes later he traded two repaired magazines for a battered detective novel.

At Bravo he sat beneath the lamp and read for three hours.

I pretended not to watch him smile at something on the page.

The next morning there was no duty roster on the wall.

There was a book on his side of the bed.

I liked that better.
